summary: Comparative analysis of our chess.h (1988 lines, two-phase action, rich reward shaping) vs fighter chess.h (958 lines, single-phase from*64+to action, minimal reward). Our engine is a significant superset of fighter. The fighter is simpler but both share the same core approach: array-based board[64], loop-based pseudo-legal movegen + legality filter, loop-based is_square_attacked. Neither uses bitboards or magic numbers. The primary gaps are: (1) our position hash is weak XOR vs proper Zobrist, (2) we lack find_king caching, (3) no bitboard-based attack maps in either engine. Since the fighter ALSO uses the array/loop approach, the gap is smaller than expected.
assumptions: ASSUMPTION-1: Fighter does NOT use bitboards. Both engines use int8_t board[64] array representation with loop-based move generation. The fighter is not a bitboard engine.
ASSUMPTION-2: Fighter does NOT use Zobrist hashing. The fighter has no position hashing or repetition detection at all (no GAME_REPETITION code).
ASSUMPTION-3: Fighter does NOT use magic attack tables. Both engines use identical ray-scanning loops for sliders (bishop/rook/queen).
ASSUMPTION-4: Fighter has no legal move caching. Our engine adds a cache keyed by position hash.
ASSUMPTION-5: Fighter has no FEN parser. Our engine supports FEN-based curriculum learning.
ASSUMPTION-6: Fighter has no SEE (Static Exchange Evaluation). Our engine has a full SEE implementation.
ASSUMPTION-7: Fighter has no reward shaping. It uses only win/loss/draw +1/-1/0 plus illegal_move_penalty and step_penalty.
ASSUMPTION-8: Fighter uses single-phase action (from*64+to = 4096 actions). Our engine uses two-phase (97 actions: pick piece then pick destination).
ASSUMPTION-9: Fighter's obs is 72 bytes (64 board + 8 metadata). Our obs is 301 bytes with validity masks.
ASSUMPTION-10: Fighter auto-queens all promotions. Our engine supports explicit underpromotion via action encoding.
ASSUMPTION-11: Fighter resets logs per-episode (log.x = value). Our engine accumulates across episodes (log.x += value) with log.n counter.

changes.title: Replace weak XOR hash with Zobrist hashing
changes.description: Our compute_position_hash (lines 571-581) uses a weak XOR-shift scheme: hash ^= board[i] << ((i%8)*8) ^ board[i] << ((i/8)*7). This produces collisions at non-trivial rates, which poisons our threefold repetition detection and legal move cache. Replace with proper Zobrist hashing: pre-computed random 64-bit keys for each (piece, square) pair plus keys for castling rights, en passant file, and side to move. Update hash incrementally in apply_move_ex instead of recomputing from scratch each time.
files_affected: csrc/chess.h:1000-1024 (generate_legal_moves_cached - uses hash as cache key)
csrc/chess.h:1028-1049 (has_any_legal_move - uses hash as cache key)
acceptance_criteria: Zobrist table: static uint64_t ZOBRIST_PIECE[13][64], ZOBRIST_CASTLE[16], ZOBRIST_EP[8], ZOBRIST_SIDE initialized from a fixed PRNG seed
Incremental update: apply_move_ex XORs out moved piece from old square, XORs in piece at new square, updates castling/ep/side keys
ChessEnv gains a uint64_t zobrist_hash field, updated incrementally
compute_position_hash becomes a full-board recompute (fallback/init only), used in c_reset
position_history stores incrementally-maintained hash values
Perft test: run perft(1..5) from starting position and several known FEN positions, verify move counts match known values (proves hash does not break move generation or game state)
Collision test: play 10000 random games, verify zero false repetition detections by cross-checking with a from-scratch hash recompute
Legal move cache test: verify cache hit rate > 90% during normal play (incremental hash matches recomputed hash)
changes.notes: Fighter has NO hashing at all - it doesn't detect threefold repetition (no GAME_REPETITION constant). Our engine already tracks repetition; we just need a better hash. The Zobrist approach is standard and well-understood. Key decisions: (a) use a compile-time PRNG seed for reproducibility, (b) store hash in ChessEnv struct, (c) update in apply_move_ex for all board changes including castling rook moves and en passant captures.

changes.title: Cache king square positions to avoid linear scans
changes.description: find_king (lines 693-699) does a linear scan of all 64 squares every call. It is called from is_in_check, which is called from: is_move_legal (per pseudo-legal move), check_game_end, write_observations (4 times for both players' check status), and process_player_action. In a typical step with ~30 pseudo-legal moves, find_king may be called 60+ times. Add king_sq[2] to ChessEnv (indexed by player) and maintain it incrementally in apply_move_ex when a king moves.
files_affected: csrc/chess.h:1058-1149 (apply_move_ex - update king_sq on king moves)
csrc/chess.h:1666-1784 (setup_from_fen - scan and set king_sq after parsing)
acceptance_criteria: find_king returns env->king_sq[player] in O(1) without any loop
king_sq updated correctly after king moves, including castling (e.g., 4->6 for white kingside)
Perft test: all perft counts unchanged after this change
Assertion: in debug builds, verify find_king_scan(env, player) == env->king_sq[player] after every move
changes.notes: Fighter also does linear scan for find_king (lines 260-266), so this is not a parity issue but a clear performance win. The two-phase action system means we call find_king much more often than fighter does.

changes.title: Pre-compute piece lists to avoid full-board scans in movegen
changes.description: generate_pseudo_legal_moves (lines 721-918) iterates all 64 squares and checks is_own_piece for each. In a typical midgame position, only ~16 of 64 squares have our pieces. Maintain piece lists: for each player, an array of (square, piece_type) pairs and a count. Update incrementally in apply_move_ex on moves, captures, promotions. This cuts the outer loop from 64 iterations to ~16.
files_affected: csrc/chess.h:97-158 (ChessEnv struct - add piece list arrays)
csrc/chess.h:721-918 (generate_pseudo_legal_moves - iterate piece list instead of board)
csrc/chess.h:1058-1149 (apply_move_ex - update piece lists on move/capture/promotion)
acceptance_criteria: Piece lists correctly maintained through all move types: normal, capture, en passant, castling, promotion
generate_pseudo_legal_moves iterates only over own pieces, not all 64 squares
Perft test: all perft counts unchanged
compute_material_score and compute_positional_score can also use piece lists for O(n_pieces) instead of O(64)
changes.notes: Fighter also scans all 64 squares (line 292). This is an improvement beyond fighter parity. The tricky part is correctly handling all the edge cases in apply_move_ex: en passant removes a pawn from a different square than to_sq; castling moves a rook; promotion changes piece type. Need careful bookkeeping.

changes.title: Optimize is_move_legal with pinned-piece detection
changes.description: is_move_legal (lines 921-977) does make-move / is_in_check / unmake-move for every pseudo-legal move. is_in_check calls find_king + is_square_attacked (which scans all attack directions). For ~30 pseudo-legal moves, this is ~30 make/unmake cycles with full attack detection each time. Optimization: (1) with king_sq cached (ENG-02), save one scan; (2) compute pinned pieces mask before the loop - a piece is pinned if it lies on a line between own king and an enemy slider. Non-pinned, non-king pieces that don't touch the king's line can skip the legality check entirely. King moves still need full check. En passant needs special handling (discovered check through the captured pawn's rank).
acceptance_criteria: Compute pinned pieces set once before iterating pseudo-legal moves
Non-king, non-pinned piece moves skip the make/unmake legality check
Pinned piece moves only need to verify they stay on the pin line
King moves still do full is_square_attacked check
En passant moves always do full legality check (horizontal pin edge case)
Perft test: all perft counts unchanged
Benchmark: measure movegen time before and after on 1000 random positions
changes.notes: This is a significant optimization that neither engine currently has. The make/unmake approach is correct but slow. A pinned-piece pre-computation can eliminate 70-80% of legality checks. This is a step towards more sophisticated move generation without going full bitboard.

changes.title: Optimize is_square_attacked with early-exit and attack-from tables
changes.description: is_square_attacked (lines 613-690) checks all 6 attack types sequentially. For legality checking during movegen, we only need to know if the king square is attacked. Optimizations: (1) Reorder attack checks by likelihood (knights and pawns first - they're the most common checks); (2) Use precomputed ATTACK_FROM[64][64] lookup: for any pair of squares, store whether an attack ray exists and what piece type could attack along it. This turns slider attack checks from ray-scanning loops into O(1) lookups when checking specific attacker squares.
acceptance_criteria: Attack detection produces identical results for all positions
Measurable speedup in perft benchmarks (target: 20-30% faster)
Perft test: all counts unchanged
changes.notes: Both engines have identical is_square_attacked implementations. This optimization helps both but is more impactful for our engine due to the two-phase system calling it more frequently. An ATTACK_FROM table would be 64*64=4096 bytes - very cache-friendly.

changes.title: Add bitboard-based attack maps for long-term performance
changes.description: Both engines currently use loop-based ray scanning for slider attacks. The ultimate performance ceiling requires bitboard representation: uint64_t per piece type, with magic number-based attack generation for bishops and rooks. This would replace the inner loops in generate_pseudo_legal_moves and is_square_attacked with O(1) bitboard operations. This is a large structural change.
files_affected: csrc/chess.h (nearly all move generation and attack detection functions)
acceptance_criteria: Bitboard representation coexists with or replaces board[64] array
Magic attack tables for bishops and rooks
Precomputed knight and king attack tables (64-entry uint64_t arrays)
Pawn attack tables (2*64 entries for white/black)
generate_pseudo_legal_moves uses bitboard iteration
is_square_attacked uses bitboard attack maps
Perft test: all counts unchanged
Benchmark: 3-5x speedup over current implementation in perft
changes.notes: This is a P2 because fighter does NOT use bitboards either, so it's beyond parity. However, it's the standard approach for high-performance chess engines and would provide the largest performance gain. Should only be attempted after P0/P1 items are done and profiled. Could adapt an existing bitboard implementation (e.g., from Stockfish) for the attack tables.

changes.title: Add comprehensive perft test suite
changes.description: Neither engine has a perft test. Perft (performance test, move path enumeration) is the gold standard for chess move generation correctness. Implement a perft function and test harness that verifies move counts from multiple known positions at multiple depths. This is prerequisite to safely making any engine changes.
acceptance_criteria: perft(depth, env) recursively counts leaf nodes at given depth
Test positions include: starting position (perft 1-5), Kiwipete, position 3-6 from chess programming wiki
Starting position perft values: depth 1=20, 2=400, 3=8902, 4=197281, 5=4865609
All known perft positions pass
Can be run as: gcc -O2 test_perft.c -o test_perft && ./test_perft
Reports time per position for benchmarking
changes.notes: This is the FIRST thing that should be implemented before any engine changes. It acts as a regression test for all subsequent modifications. Fighter also lacks perft tests. The perft function itself is trivial: generate legal moves, for each move apply/recurse/undo, return count.

changes.title: Optimize legal move cache with incremental Zobrist hash
changes.description: generate_legal_moves_cached (lines 1000-1024) and has_any_legal_move (lines 1028-1049) use compute_position_hash as cache key, which recomputes from scratch every call (O(64) for board scan). After ENG-01 (Zobrist hashing), this becomes O(1) since the hash is maintained incrementally. Additionally, the cache is invalidated too often because the weak hash may not match after complex move sequences. With proper Zobrist, cache hit rates should improve significantly.
acceptance_criteria: Cache key uses env->zobrist_hash instead of compute_position_hash(env)
Cache lookup is O(1)
Cache hit rate > 95% when position hasn't changed between calls in same step
No behavioral change in game outcomes
changes.notes: This is a direct consequence of ENG-01. Once we have incremental Zobrist, the cache becomes much more effective. Fighter has no caching at all.

changes.title: Eliminate redundant material/positional score recomputation
changes.description: process_player_action (lines 1362-1364, 1412-1421) calls compute_material_score and compute_positional_score before and after each move. Each scans all 64 squares. With piece lists (ENG-03), this becomes O(n_pieces) but could be further optimized by maintaining running totals incrementally in apply_move_ex.
acceptance_criteria: Material and positional scores maintained incrementally
Score deltas computed in O(1) per move instead of O(64)
Scores verified against from-scratch recomputation in debug builds
No change in reward values
changes.notes: Fighter has no reward shaping, so this is our-engine-only optimization. The material/positional score functions are only called when reward_material/reward_position configs are non-zero, so this is only impactful when those features are enabled.

changes.title: Reduce observation write overhead
changes.description: write_observations (lines 1519-1620) calls generate_legal_moves_cached (via compute_valid_pieces_mask and compute_valid_dests_mask) and is_in_check (4 calls: self/opp for both players). The legal move generation is cached but the valid_pieces/valid_dests computation scans the legal move list twice. Optimization: (1) compute valid_pieces mask during legal move generation itself; (2) cache is_in_check result since it doesn't change within a step.
acceptance_criteria: Observation values identical before and after optimization
is_in_check called at most once per player per step
Valid pieces mask computed during movegen pass, not separately
changes.notes: Fighter's write_observations is much simpler (lines 707-767) - just 72 bytes with no validity masks. Our 301-byte observation with masks is more expensive but provides the agent with richer information for the two-phase action system.

changes.title: Benchmark framework for engine performance comparison
changes.description: Create a benchmark harness that measures: (1) perft nodes/second at various depths, (2) legal move generation time per position, (3) is_square_attacked calls per step, (4) average step time in self-play. This enables data-driven optimization decisions and tracks progress across ENG-01 through ENG-10.
acceptance_criteria: Measures perft(5) from starting position in nodes/sec
Measures average generate_legal_moves time over 10000 random positions
Measures average c_step time over 1000 complete random games
Outputs results in machine-parseable format (JSON or CSV)
Can compare before/after for each optimization
changes.notes: Essential for validating that optimizations actually improve performance. Without benchmarks, we're optimizing blind.

board_representation.ours: int8_t board[64], array-based, same as fighter

move_generation.ours: Loop-based pseudo-legal + is_move_legal filter (make/unmake), with legal move caching (lines 721-1049)
move_generation.fighter: Identical loop-based pseudo-legal + is_move_legal filter, no caching (lines 288-563)
move_generation.gap: We are AHEAD (have caching). Both lack pin-based optimization.

position_hashing.ours: Weak XOR hash with shift patterns (lines 571-581), used for repetition detection and move cache
position_hashing.fighter: NO hashing at all, no repetition detection
position_hashing.gap: We have more features but our hash quality is poor. Need Zobrist.

move_encoding.ours: Internal: from*64+to (0-4095). External: two-phase 97 actions (pick piece, pick destination/promotion)
move_encoding.fighter: Single-phase from*64+to (4096 actions) for both internal and external
move_encoding.gap: Different design choices. Our two-phase is more RL-friendly (smaller action space) but adds complexity.

move_application.gap: We support underpromotion. Fighter always auto-queens.

observations.ours: 301 bytes: board(64) + metadata(7) + phase(2) + selected_piece(64) + valid_pieces(64) + valid_dests(64) + valid_promos(32) + check(2) + rule50(1) + pass(1)
observations.gap: Our obs is richer for two-phase action system. Fighter relies on agent learning implicit validity.

game_rules.ours: Checkmate, stalemate, 50-move, insufficient material, threefold repetition (with toggles)
game_rules.fighter: Checkmate, stalemate, 50-move, insufficient material (no repetition detection)

reward_system.ours: Win/loss/draw + configurable: invalid_piece/move, capture_bonus, check_bonus, material_delta, positional_delta, castling, repetition_penalty, SEE/hanging, draw_reward
reward_system.gap: We have dramatically richer reward shaping. Fighter is minimal.

struct_size.ours: ~5KB+ (board + phase_state[2] + position_history[512] + legal_moves_cache[256] + all reward configs)
struct_size.gap: Our struct is much larger. May affect cache performance with many parallel envs.

priority_order: ENG-07: Perft test suite (FIRST - safety net for all other changes)
ENG-01: Zobrist hashing (fixes correctness issue with repetition/cache)
ENG-02: King square caching (easy win, prerequisite for ENG-04)
ENG-11: Benchmark framework (enables measuring impact of changes)
ENG-08: Optimize legal move cache with Zobrist (quick win after ENG-01)
ENG-04: Pinned-piece optimization (significant speedup for legality checking)
ENG-03: Piece lists (moderate speedup for movegen and scoring)
ENG-09: Incremental material/positional scores (small speedup when reward shaping enabled)
ENG-06: Bitboard migration (large effort, large reward, long-term)
